title: Where did you all go?
goal: Ask a group of friends where they went and who with, using the you-all past ending -tu.
grammar: Past tense I: you all (-tu); we (-na) recycled
tip: For a group the ending is -tu 'you all' (you met -na 'we' in s1u036). Take the 'I' form and add -u: wiṣalt → wiṣaltu? (did you all arrive?); riḥt → riḥtu; ṭilaʿt → ṭilaʿtu. Use it for two or more people, men or women.
dialogue: Hi there! When did you (all) get here?
هلا والله! وصلنا قبل شوي. وانت؟
hala wallāh! wiṣalna gabil shwayy. w inta?
Hi! We got here a little while ago. And you?
أنا وصلت الحين. وين طلعتوا البارحة؟
ana wiṣalt il-ḥīn. wēn ṭilaʿtu l-bārḥa?
I've just got here. Where did you go out last night?
We went to the beach, and we got back late.
Really? Who did you go with?
ويا ربعنا. المرة الثانية تروح ويانا!
wiyya rabʿna. il-marra th-thānya trūḥ wiyyāna!
With our friends. Next time you're coming with us!
items: to one man: wiṣalt; to one woman: wiṣalti; you'll see written وصلتو
to one man: ṭilaʿt; to one woman: ṭilaʿti
to one man: riḥt; to one woman: riḥti

title: Where is everyone?
goal: Ask a colleague where everyone went, and understand what they did and didn't do.
grammar: Past tense I: they (-aw, written ـوا); ma + past
tip: 'They' adds -aw, written ـوا: rāḥ (he went) → rāḥaw (they went). A short vowel before it drops: kitab (he wrote) → kitbaw, wiṣal → wiṣlaw, rijaʿ → rijʿaw. For 'didn't', put ma in front: ma kitbaw (they didn't write).
dialogue: صباح الخير يا مريم. وين الكل؟
ṣabāḥ il-khēr yā Maryam. wēn il-kill?
Good morning, Maryam. Where is everyone?
صباح النور. وصلوا الصبح وراحوا الاجتماع
ṣabāḥ in-nūr. wiṣlaw iṣ-ṣubḥ w rāḥaw il-ijtimāʿ
Good morning. They got in this morning and went to the meeting.
Really? They didn't write me anything!
They wrote in the group yesterday.
Sorry! Did they go a long time ago?
No, a little while ago. Look, they're back!
items: a long time ago; for a long time

title: Good news!
goal: Ask what happened, congratulate a friend and answer, and say what you said, saw and slept.
grammar: Past tense II: hollow verbs (gilt, shift, nimt)
tip: Verbs with a long middle vowel (gāl said, shāf saw, nām slept) shorten it before -t: gilt (I said, you said), shift, nimt. To a woman add -i: gilti, shifti. The he-form keeps the long vowel: gāl, shāf, ṣār (it happened).
culture: Say mabrūk for any good news: a passed exam, a new job, a wedding, a new car. The reply is allāh ybārik fīk (to a woman: fīch). When admiring something new, or a child, people add mā shāʼ allāh.
dialogue: الله يبارك فيك. قلت لك بنجح!
Thanks. I told you I'd pass!
إي، قلت لي. متى شفت النتيجة؟
Yes, you told me. When did you see the result?
il-bārḥa s-sāʿa thalāth, w ma nimt!
Last night at three, and I didn't sleep!
items: to a woman: allāh ybārik fīch (فيج)
I said; you said (to a man)
I saw; you saw (to a man)
I slept; you slept (to a man)
I passed; you passed (to a man)

title: What did you do yesterday?
goal: Tell a colleague what you did yesterday and ask her, with sawwēt, ligēt and mishēt.
grammar: Past tense II: defective verbs (sawwēt, ligēt, mishēt)
tip: Verbs that end in a vowel (sawwa did, liga found, misha walked) add -ē- before -t: sawwēt (I did, you did), ligēt, mishēt. To a woman: sawwēti, ligēti. 'Didn't' is ma + verb: ma sawwēt shay (I didn't do anything).
dialogue: Good morning. What did you do yesterday?
صباح النور. مشيت في السوق وايد
ṣabāḥ in-nūr. mishēt fi s-sūg wāyid
Good morning. I walked round the souq for ages.
Really? Did you find anything nice?
hē, ligēt maṭʿam ḥilu. w inti?
Yes, I found a nice restaurant. And you?
أنا؟ ما سويت شي. نمت طول اليوم!
ana? ma sawwēt shay. nimt ṭūl il-yōm!
Me? I didn't do anything. I slept all day!
items: I did; you did (to a man)
what did you do? (to a man)
I found; you found (to a man)
I walked; you walked (to a man)
to a woman: mishēti (مشيتي); also means 'I left, I set off'
good for you, you did the right thing (to a man)

title: Where did you put the key?
goal: Tell Sēf where you put the car key and who took it, and say whether you've eaten: ḥaṭṭēt, khadht, kalt.
grammar: Past tense II: doubled and hamzated verbs (ḥaṭṭēt, khadht, kalt)
tip: Doubled verbs (ḥaṭṭ put) add -ē- like sawwēt: ḥaṭṭēt (I put, you put). 'Take' and 'eat' have short forms: khadh (he took) → khadht (I took), kal (he ate) → kalt (I ate). To a woman: ḥaṭṭēti, khadhti, kalti.
dialogue: Where did you put the car key?
I put the key on the table.
Maybe your brother took the key?
آسف، أنا خذت المفتاح! يلا، كلت شي؟
āsif, ana khadht il-miftāḥ! yalla, kalt shay?
Sorry, I took the key! Right, have you eaten anything?
No, I haven't eaten since the morning.
items: I put; you put (to a man)
I took; you took (to a man)
to a woman: khadhti (خذتي); khadhat 'she took' is spelled the same; also said: khadhēt (خذيت)
I ate; you ate (to a man)
to a woman: kalti (كلتي); also said: akalt (أكلت), kalēt (كليت)
I haven't eaten, I didn't eat

title: I brought you something
goal: Arrive at Sēf's family home, greet Umm Sēf, say how you came and what you brought, and ask after Sēf.
grammar: Past tense II: come and bring (yīt, yibt, ma yā)
tip: 'Come' and 'bring' are irregular: yīt (I came, you came), yā (he came), ma yā (he didn't come, he hasn't come); yibt (I brought, you brought), yāb (he brought). Emiratis say y where fuṣḥā and many other speakers have j (jīt, jibt), so these are written with ي.
dialogue: Thank you. I brought you all some sweets.
ما قصرت، بس ما في داعي!
mā gaṣṣart, bas ma fī dāʿi!
That's very kind, but there was no need!
ما سوينا شي. سيف هني، الله يخليج؟
mā sawwēna shay. Sēf hni, allāh ykhallīch?
It's nothing. Is Sēf in, please?
ما يا من الجامعة. ييت ويا منو؟
ma yā min il-jāmʿa. yīt wiyya minu?
He hasn't come back from the university yet. Who did you come with?
I came on my own, by taxi.
items: I came; you came (to a man)
to a woman: yīti (ييتي); Kuwait: jīt (جيت)
I brought; you brought (to a man)
to a woman: yibti (يبتي); Kuwait: jibt (جبت)
to a woman: yibt-lich (يبت لج); to a group or a family: yibt-lkum (يبت لكم)
he didn't come; he hasn't come
you'll see written مافي داعي; also very common: ma lah dāʿi (ما له داعي, you'll see written ماله داعي)
it was nothing (reply to mā gaṣṣart)

title: Checkpoint 1.2: Sēf's weekend
goal: Follow Sēf's story of a weekend in the desert and ask about it, using the past for other people.
tip: Review: the past endings you know, now for other people. We: sawwēna, shifna. You all: sawwētu, nimtu. He: yāb (brought), gāl (said). She: gālat. The -ē- of sawwēt stays: sawwēna, sawwētu.
dialogue: هلا سيف! شو سويت في الويكند؟
hala Sēf! shu sawwēt fi l-wīkind?
Hi Sēf! What did you do at the weekend?
We went out to the desert. My dad brought the tent.
Nice! And what did you do there?
We made tea, and we looked at the stars.
mā shāʼ allāh! w nimtu hnāk?
Wonderful! And did you sleep out there?
No, my mum said: we have to go back!
items: to one man: sawwēt; to one woman: sawwēti
to one man: nimt; to one woman: nimti

title: Which day?
goal: On a late-night call, pick a day to go out with a friend, name the days of the week, and say good night.
grammar: Days of the week: yōm + day
tip: Days come with yōm 'day': yōm il-aḥad (Sun), il-ithnēn (Mon), ith-thalātha (Tue), il-arbaʿa (Wed), il-khamīs (Thu), il-jumʿa (Fri), is-sabt (Sat). yōm can be dropped, and no word for 'on' is needed: (yōm) il-jumʿa ʿindi shughul (on Friday I've got work).
culture: Since January 2022 the UAE's official weekend has been Saturday and Sunday, and federal government offices close at Friday noon (Sharjah's government takes Friday off too). Kuwait's weekend is Friday and Saturday. Friday's noon prayer is the main prayer of the week, so Friday plans usually start after it.
dialogue: Shall we go to the beach this week?
Friday I've got work. Another day?
زين، يوم السبت. تصبح على خير!
zēn, yōm is-sabt. tiṣbaḥ ʿala khēr!
items: nrūḥ il-baḥar? = shall we go to the beach?
to a woman: tiṣbaḥīn ʿala khēr (تصبحين على خير); reply: w inta min ahlah
reply to good night (to a man)
to a woman: w inti min ahlah

title: Mornings and afternoons
goal: Compare your day with a colleague's: morning, midday, afternoon, evening and night.
grammar: Parts of the day: iṣ-ṣubḥ, iẓ-ẓuhur, il-ʿaṣr, il-lēl
tip: Most parts of the day need no word for 'in': iṣ-ṣubḥ ashtaghil (in the morning I work), il-ʿaṣr fi l-jāmʿa (in the afternoon at the university). Night usually takes one: fi l-lēl (at night). Plans are often timed by prayers: baʿd il-maghrib.
culture: The five prayers frame the day: il-fajr (dawn), iẓ-ẓuhur (midday), il-ʿaṣr (afternoon), il-maghrib (sunset), il-ʿisha (night). People often set times by them ('after ʿaṣr', 'before maghrib'), and the clock times move with the seasons: in Dubai, maghrib is about 5:30 pm in winter and about 7 pm in summer.
dialogue: Maryam, do you only work mornings?
la, iṣ-ṣubḥ w il-ʿaṣr. w inta?
No, mornings and afternoons. And you?
أنا هني الصبح، والعصر في الجامعة
ana hni ṣ-ṣubḥ, w il-ʿaṣr fi l-jāmʿa
I'm here in the mornings, and at the university in the afternoons.
mā shāʼ allāh! w mita tirtāḥ?
Wow! And when do you rest?
زين. يلا، نتغدى ويا الكل الظهر؟
zēn. yalla, nitghadda wiyya l-kill iẓ-ẓuhur?
Good. Shall we have lunch with everyone at midday?
items: the late afternoon; in the afternoon
at night: fi l-lēl; also said: bil-lēl (بالليل)
we have lunch; shall we have lunch?

title: What time is the film?
goal: Tell the time with half past, quarter past and quarter to, and count minutes, before a film with Sēf.
grammar: Telling the time (w nuṣṣ, w rubʿ, illa rubʿ); a singular noun after 11
tip: is-sāʿa + hour: is-sāʿa thintēn (two o'clock), is-sāʿa waḥda (one). Then w nuṣṣ (half past), w rubʿ (quarter past), illa rubʿ (quarter to). From 11 up the noun stays singular: ʿishrīn dagīga, khamsīn dirham, but khams dagāyig.
dialogue: w il-film is-sāʿa thalāth illa rubʿ!
And the film's at quarter to three!
يعني بعد ربع ساعة؟ والتذكرة بكم؟
yaʿni baʿd rubʿ sāʿa? w it-tadhkara b-cham?
So in a quarter of an hour? And how much is the ticket?
بخمسين درهم. والسينما عشرين دقيقة من هني!
b-khamsīn dirham. w is-sīnama ʿishrīn dagīga min hni!
Fifty dirhams. And the cinema's twenty minutes from here!
Come on, quick! We're late every time.
items: a quarter: rubʿ (ربع), as in rubʿ sāʿa; quarter to: illa rubʿ
3 to 10 take the plural (khams dagāyig); 11 and up the singular (ʿishrīn dagīga)
we're late (as a habit), we get late
I: atʼakhkhar (أتأخر); late right now: taʼakhkharna 'we're late', taʼakhkhart 'I'm late'
